item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

23 Sep 2026, 12:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Brad Penner)
Drew Rasmussen allowed one hit in 6 2/3 outstanding innings and the visiting Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East with a 6-1 victory over the New York Yankees on Tuesday night in the nightcap of a day-night doubleheader.
The Rays won for the 20th time in 28 games and clinched their fifth division title. Tampa Bay last won the AL East in 2021 when it won a team-record 100 games. Yandy Diaz drove in four runs on a pair of singles.
Rasmussen (16-5) took a no-hitter into the seventh until Heliot Ramos opened the inning with a double to left for New York. Ramos eventually scored on an RBI single by rookie George Lombard Jr. off Kevin Kelly.
Rasmussen finished with 11 strikeouts for his fourth career double-digit strikeout performance. He finished two shy of his career-high set June 10 against the Boston Red Sox and the Rays won his 12th consecutive start.
Yankees 2, Rays 0 (Game 1)
Cody Bellinger hit a two-run home run in the fourth inning as host New York recorded a shutout over Tampa Bay in the opener of a day-night doubleheader.
With the victory, the Yankees temporarily prevented the Rays from clinching the AL East and moved six games ahead of the Boston Red Sox for the American League's top wild-card spot.
New York's Carlos Rodon (7-3) scattered three singles over eight innings as the Yankees finished off the victory in a brisk 2 hours, 2 minutes. Rodon struck out eight in his 100th career win and also reached 1,500 strikeouts for his career. Rays right-hander Nick Martinez (15-5) allowed two runs on five hits over six innings with seven strikeouts to take his first loss since July 9.
Dodgers 7, Padres 0
Freddie Freeman drove in three runs, Will Smith and Tommy Edman hit home runs, and Los Angeles inched closer to the best record in the National League with a shutout of visiting San Diego.
Eight Dodgers pitchers held down the red-hot Padres offense in a bullpen game, with Justin Wrobleski (12-5) earning the win. Roki Sasaki struck out two in one inning in his return from a blister issue. The Dodgers extended their home winning streak to 11 games.
Los Angeles moved to within one game of the NL-best Milwaukee Brewers and reduced its magic number for a top-two NL spot and a bye into the National League Division Series to one. Luis Campusano had two hits for the Padres, whose magic number to clinch a playoff spot remained at two.
Phillies 6, Brewers 4
Bryson Stott delivered the tiebreaking hit in the eighth inning to guide Philadelphia to a victory over visiting Milwaukee. Brandon Marsh homered and knocked in three runs as the Phillies lowered their magic number to two to clinch a postseason berth.
Zack Wheeler ended up with a no-decision after striking out 11 while giving up three runs and five hits in 5 2/3 innings. Wheeler struck out the first seven batters he faced, setting a Phillies record for consecutive strikeouts to begin a game. His first-inning strikeout of Brice Turang was the 2,000th of his career.
The Brewers saw their lead over the Dodgers for the top record in the majors shrink to one as they lost just the third time in their last 13 games. William Contreras knocked in three runs.
Marlins 8, Cubs 2 (12 innings)
Griffin Conine plated the go-ahead run that ignited a six-run 12th inning for visiting Miami, which snapped a three-game losing by beating Chicago and postponing the Cubs' playoff celebration for at least a day.
On a night when runs were scarce until the final inning, both teams endured a pair of scoreless extra frames before Conine broke the drought with a leadoff, golf-shot single off Caleb Thielbar that fell just inside the left field line. Esteury Ruiz, the automatic runner, scored from second to make it 3-2 as the Marlins sent 10 batters to the plate in the inning.
The Cubs could have clinched a wild-card playoff spot with a win or Arizona loss, but neither of those happened keeping the Diamondbacks mathematically alive. Josh Ekness (3-4) struck out a pair in the 11th inning to get the win while Thielbar (3-4) gave up three runs -- two earned -- in his inning of work.
Guardians 3, Red Sox 2
Nathaniel Lowe drove in Chase DeLauter with a sacrifice fly in the ninth inning and Cleveland held on to beat host Boston in the first game of a three-game series.
Cleveland not only extended its winning streak to six but maintained its one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox for first place in the AL Central.
Parker Messick held Boston to one run on five hits in five innings, his 14th straight start allowing three runs or fewer. Payton Tolle started for the Red Sox and gave up two runs on eight hits in 5 2/3 innings as the Guardians went 1-for-12 with runners in scoring position and stranded 15.
White Sox 14, Royals 11
Chase Meidroth smacked a three-run home run among his three hits and drove in five, and Brenton Doyle, Randal Grichuk and Munetaka Murakami also homered to power Chicago past host Kansas City.
Chicago won for the fourth time in five games to remain one game behind the AL Central-leading Cleveland Guardians. The White Sox, who hold the third and final AL wild-card spot, reduced their magic number to earn a playoff berth to three.
Vinnie Pasquantino hit a ninth-inning grand slam for the Royals, who lost their fifth straight. He went 3-for-5 with a double and also drove in five.
Nationals 3, Tigers 1
CJ Abrams hit a pair of home runs and drove in all three runs as visiting Washington topped Detroit. Abrams reached 100 RBIs for the season with his solo shot in the second inning, then broke a 1-1 tie in the seventh with his 33rd long ball of the season, a two-run blast.
Dylan Crews had two hits and scored the other run for the Nationals. Rookie Jackson Kent (2-4) earned the win in long relief. He allowed one run on six hits over four innings and struck out three. Opener Riley Cornelio lasted 2 2/3 innings, striking out four and walking three.
Ben Malgeri scored the Tigers' only run. Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark each had two hits.
Pirates 2, Cardinals 0
Jared Jones and two relievers combined on a one-hitter as Pittsburgh beat visiting St. Louis for a fifth straight win. Jones (5-6) lowered his ERA to 1.08 in four September starts and struck out nine with zero walks over seven innings while throwing 63 of his 86 pitches for strikes.
Pittsburgh broke a scoreless tie with two outs in the sixth inning on Ryan O'Hearn's RBI single against Andre Pallante (12-8). Pallante allowed one run on three hits with two walks and two strikeouts over six innings.
St. Louis struck out 14 times and lost for the fifth time in its last six games.
Astros 7, Mariners 0
Christian Walker hit a three-run home run, Yordan Alvarez launched a two-run homer and Isaac Paredes added a solo shot as Houston slugged and pitched its way past host Seattle.
Jose Altuve, Yainer Diaz, Alvarez and Paredes each collected two hits for the Astros, who pulled into a first-place tie with the Texas Rangers in the West. Five Astros pitchers combined to throw a four-hit shutout. Miguel Ullola (1-0) earned his first major league win, allowing one hit and striking out two over two innings of relief.
Julio Rodriguez notched two hits for Seattle. The Mariners went 0-for-3 with runners in scoring position and stranded nine.
Reds 4, Braves 0
Brandon Williamson fired six scoreless innings and Cincinnati supported him with three solo homers to defeat host Atlanta in the opener of a three-game series.
Cincinnati ended a two-game losing streak and evened the season series with Atlanta at 2-2. Williamson (5-4) worked six scoreless innings, allowing three hits and two strikeouts. Elly De La Cruz (29), Dane Myers (8) and Eugenio Suarez (25) each hit a home run for the Reds. It was Suarez's 350th career homer, making him the 10th active player to reach that mark.
Atlanta starter JR Ritchie (1-4) pitched five innings and allowed one run on four hits and three walks. The rookie struck out a career-high eight batters.
Mets 6, Rangers 3
Francisco Alvarez laced a go-ahead two-run double in the sixth, then scored an insurance run on an unusual sacrifice fly for visiting New York, who damaged Texas' playoff hopes with a win in the opener of a three-game interleague series in Arlington.
Juan Soto had an RBI single in the third, and Carson Benge capped the scoring with a run-scoring double in the seventh for the Mets. The club won hours after removing the interim tag from manager Andy Green and signing him to a three-year extension.
Josh Jung had an RBI double in the third, and Elias Diaz and Wyatt Langford lofted sacrifice flies in the fourth for the Rangers, who entered Tuesday with a one-game lead over the Houston Astros in the AL West.
Diamondbacks 7, Rockies 2
Nolan Arenado homered and doubled among his three hits, Michael Soroka tossed seven strong innings, and Arizona kept its slim postseason hopes alive with a win over host Colorado in Denver.
Geraldo Perdomo also had three hits and Ildemaro Vargas finished with two hits for Arizona, which remains alive in the NL wild-card race, sitting four games behind Philadelphia, San Diego and the Chicago Cubs for the third and final spot with five games to go.
Mickey Moniak homered for Colorado, which finished with just three hits and just one after the third inning. The Rockies (57-100) are the first team to lose 100 or more games in four straight seasons since the 1962-65 New York Mets.
Twins 3, Giants 2
Walker Jenkins homered, Luke Keaschall contributed both offensively and defensively, and Minnesota evened its road interleague series against San Francisco.
Taj Bradley (12-6) combined with four relievers on a six-hitter for the Twins, who used two late diving catches by Keaschall in right field to prevent the Giants from taking the first two of the series.
Bradley allowed just one other hit -- a fifth-inning single by Drew Gilbert -- in his six innings. He walked three and struck out six. Keaschall's one-out triple scored Ryan Kreidler, then Brooks Lee gave Minnesota the lead for good with a run-scoring single to plate Keaschall.
A's 9, Angels 7
Carlos Cortes hit a go-ahead two-run homer in the bottom of the eighth inning and the Athletics overcame a six-run deficit to beat Los Angeles in West Sacramento, Calif.
In addition to the homer off Sam Bachman, Cortes also delivered a pinch-hit RBI triple in the seventh, helping the Athletics end a six-game losing streak. Zack Gelof hit a two-run homer later in the eighth for the A's. Shea Langeliers and Lawrence Butler each had three hits and an RBI for the Athletics.
Denzer Guzman homered and drove in four RBIs for the Angels, who have lost four of their last six games. Mike Trout added three hits and two runs for Los Angeles (60-97), which has never lost 100 games in a season.
Blue Jays at Orioles, ppd.
The scheduled game between Toronto and host Baltimore was postponed due to ongoing inclement weather. The game will be made up as part of a split doubleheader on Wednesday, with games starting at 1:35 p.m. and 6:35 p.m. ET.

(Photo credit: Joe Nicholson)
Christian Walker hit a three-run home run, Yordan Alvarez launched a two-run homer and Isaac Paredes added a solo shot as the visiting Houston Astros slugged their way to a 7-0 victory over the Seattle Mariners on Tuesday.
Jose Altuve, Yainer Diaz, Alvarez and Paredes each collected two hits for the Astros (78-79), who pulled into a first-place tie with the Texas Rangers in the American League West. Houston owns the head-to-head tiebreaker over Texas, so would win the division if the teams remain tied at the end of the season.
Five Astros pitchers combined to throw a four-hit shutout. Miguel Ullola (1-0) earned his first major league win, allowing one hit and striking out two over two innings.
Julio Rodriguez notched two hits for Seattle (73-84). The Mariners went 0-for-3 with runners in scoring position and stranded nine.
Jeremy Pena led off the game with an infield single to shortstop, stole second, and scored on Alvarez's single to right. It marked the 100th RBI of the season for Alvarez, the second time in his career he's reached that milestone. Paredes and Altuve followed with singles, loading the bases with no outs.
Seattle starter Logan Gilbert (12-11) escaped the first-inning jam when Diaz struck out looking before Walker and Taylor Trammell flied out.
Altuve and Diaz opened the third with back-to-back singles before Walker launched his 26th home run of the season and the 200th of his career, a three-run shot to deep left, giving the Astros a 4-0 lead.
In the fifth, J.P. Crawford drew a one-out walk. After Randy Arozarena struck out swinging, Dominic Canzone singled to center. Crawford advanced to third, but Cal Raleigh struck out to end the inning.
Houston's advantage increased to 5-0 on Paredes' solo homer in the sixth.
With one out in the eighth, Pena was hit by a pitch, and Alvarez belted a slider over the wall in right for his 41st home run of the season, extending Houston's lead to 7-0.
Houston starter Cristian Javier tossed two shutout innings, allowing one hit and two walks while striking out two. The Astros announced Javier exited the game with groin tightness.
Gilbert gave up four runs on 10 hits over four innings, walking two and striking out three.

Injuries have started to take a toll on the Toronto Blue Jays lately. While it seemed like there was still hope for Toronto to make the postseason a couple of weeks ago, that has ultimately not turned out to be the case.
The struggles have been real, and the injuries have not made it easier. Outfielder Brett Bateman suffered a hip injury on Monday night, while first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has dealt with back tightness. Not to mention starter Trey Yesavage, who just returned from knee surgery after six weeks.
Ace Dylan Cease had been holding down the rotation recently, but even he hasn't been immune to the injury bug that has hurt the Blue Jays this season. Cease has been a lifeline to Toronto's pitching staff, but had been dealing with shoulder fatigue over the past few weeks, according to manager John Schneider.
Cease struggled mightily against the Texas Rangers on Friday, going just 2.2 innings and walking six, while giving up four runs (one earned). He went back to Toronto for an MRI and was scratched from his next start on Wednesday.
It was revealed on Monday that the MRI only showed inflammation in the right shoulder and no structural issues. Cease will not need surgery for anything more serious.
More on Cease's Injury Situation
The 30-year-old explained the news himself and the fact that he's just been diagnosed with shoulder inflammation. This isn't an issue that is expected to go into 2027 and affect his availability for next season.
It's still unlikely that Cease ends up pitching again this season with less than a week left, although that's still being determined. Given the Jays are basically out of postseason contention, there's really no need to push him.
The shoulder issue is what caused Cease's pitch velocity to go down.
“The velocity being down has been a little bit concerning,” Cease said, according to Keegan Matheson of MLB.com. "But at the same time, I’m getting outs. It wasn’t anything that was too scary because nothing about it feels like I’ve got something that needs surgery."
After his incredible complete game at the Boston Red Sox on July 25, where he threw 120 pitches, Cease didn't look as strong, even though he still ended up throwing six quality starts from that time until now.
“It’s definitely a bit heavy and achy, just not normal,” Cease said. "The last couple of starts, the velo keeps going down and down. Especially that last one, I almost felt like I was hurting the team."
It's clear that the issue caught him to him, but the fact that he pitched through it at a high level for some time shows the quality of Cease.
He has posted a 2.40 ERA in 29 starts, which is the second-lowest mark in the American League. Cease has a career-high 239 strikeouts in 169 innings pitched, with an 11-6 record.

Ronald Acuña Jr. suma su tercera temporada con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas en MLB y entra al top 3 entre venezolanos.
Ronald Acuña Jr. sigue escribiendo su nombre en la historia del béisbol venezolano. El outfielder de los Bravos de Atlanta cerró otra temporada con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas, un logro que pocos han repetido con tanta consistencia. Acuña alcanza su tercera campaña 20-20 y con eso se suma a un grupo selecto de compatriotas que marcaron época en Grandes Ligas.
El camino no fue sencillo. Las lesiones interrumpieron su ritmo en varios momentos y limitaron su presencia en la alineación. Aun así, el criollo encontró la forma de producir cuando estuvo disponible y dejó números que respaldan su calidad. Su combinación de poder y velocidad lo mantiene como una pieza clave en el ataque de Atlanta y como referencia obligada al hablar de los mejores peloteros de Venezuela.
Este hito llega en un año en el que muchos dudaban de su capacidad para mantener el nivel de años anteriores y en el que las lesiones volvieron a estar presentes. Pese a esto los números de Acuña confirman su recuperación, algo que resulta clave tomando en cuenta que nos acercamos a octubre y que Atlanta lo necesita sano para poder pelear en playoffs.
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Ronald Acuña Jr.: velocidad, poder y una nueva página en MLB
Qué significa la temporada 20-20 de Ronald Acuña Jr. en 2026
Una campaña 20-20 exige un buen desempeño en dos facetas claves de la ofensiva: pegarle fuerte a la bola y saber correr las bases con inteligencia. Acuña cumplió con ese doble requisito en 2026 y con eso llegó a su tercera temporada 20-20 en la MLB. Sus otras dos veces con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas llegaron en 2019 y 2023, años en los que también dejó un perfil ofensivo completo, con poder en el bate y presión en las bases.
Acuña acumula 103 partidos en 2026, con 454 apariciones en el plato, 102 hits, 55 carreras impulsadas y 60 anotadas. Esos números reflejan un rendimiento sólido para un jugador que pasó por dos distensiones en el corva izquierda y que en varios tramos de la temporada no estuvo al 100%. Aun con esos obstáculos, el criollo fue capaz de dejar muy buenos números en esta temporada regular.
Este tipo de registro no depende solo de fuerza. También exige una excelente lectura de lanzamientos, disciplina en el plato y timing para robar algo que lo ha caracterizado a lo largo de su carrera. Hay que recordar que Acuña suma 225 bases robadas de por vida y 206 jonrones en su carrera regular, cifras que lo ubican en un nivel distinto dentro de la ofensiva venezolana en la MLB.
El club selecto de venezolanos con temporadas 20-20 en MLB
Pocos peloteros de Venezuela han logrado una campaña 20-20. El grupo lo encabezan Bobby Abreu, Carlos González y José Altuve, tres nombres que definieron épocas distintas y que dejaron huella en sus respectivas franquicias. Acuña se une a ese trío y con su tercera vez se ubica en el top 3 histórico de jonroneros venezolanos en Grandes Ligas, un escalón que pocos alcanzan y que mide impacto real en el juego.
Bobby Abreu marcó el estándar con la marca 20-20 en 9 temporadas a lo largo de su carrera en MLB, un número que refleja su combinación de poder y velocidad durante más de una década. Carlos González alcanzó ese registro en 4 ocasiones durante sus 12 campañas en la liga mayor, con picos de producción que lo llevaron a la élite del bateo. José Altuve, por su parte, suma 3 temporadas 20-20 con los Astros de Houston, un logro que respalda su perfil de bateador de contacto con velocidad en las bases.
La marca de Acuña también tiene un componente de resistencia. Llegar tres veces a 20-20 implica mantener salud relativa y rendimiento en distintos momentos de la carrera. El criollo ya tiene un MVP en 2023, un Rookie del Año en 2018 y un récord histórico de 40-70 en esa misma campaña del MVP. Esos logros, sumados a su tercera temporada 20-20, lo convierten en referencia para la nueva generación de peloteros venezolanos.

- Bob Abreu (9)
- Carlos González (4)
- Ronald Acuña Jr. (3)
- Jackson Chourio (3)
- José Altuve (3)
- Magglio Ordóñez (1)
- Elvis Andrus (1)
MÁS INFORMACIÓN: Ronald Acuña Jr. de regreso: el venezolano de los Braves que quiere recuperar su MVP tras superar la lesión de rodilla
Por qué Ronald Acuña Jr. sigue siendo clave para los Bravos y para Venezuela
Atlanta construye su ataque alrededor de la versatilidad. Acuña ofrece poder desde la parte alta del orden al bate, capacidad para estirar hits y presión constante sobre la defensa rival. Esa combinación hace que su presencia en el lineup, incluso con minutos limitados debido a las lesiones, cambie la dinámica del juego.
Acuña apenas tiene 28 años y ya suma tres campañas 20-20, una cifra que deja espacio para seguir creciendo. Su historial de poder y velocidad, sumado a su capacidad de ajuste, lo pone en ruta para añadir más temporadas con al menos 20 jonrones y 20 bases robadas. La gran incógnita ahora es si podrá igualar o superar las 9 veces de Bobby Abreu, el récord entre venezolanos en MLB. El tiempo dirá si el criollo se acerca a esa marca o si incluso la deja atrás.

item.content:encoded:
It was late August, amid a tough series against the Arizona Diamondbacks, when Pete Crow-Armstrong found assistant hitting coach John Mallee to sit together on the bench in the visitors’ dugout at Chase Field.
The Chicago Cubs were on the verge of losing a second consecutive close game, and Crow-Armstrong had, to that point, an 0-fer series. Crow-Armstrong needed to talk out his frustrations. Mallee listened, as always. It’s become a common sight during each half-inning the Cubs are batting: Crow-Armstrong posted up next to Mallee along the dugout railing, chatting while watching the game.
Their bond dates to 2023, when Mallee served as hitting coach at Triple-A Iowa during Crow-Armstrong’s first time reaching that level. They worked together there in 2024 when the center fielder spent the first three weeks of the season in Iowa and again for a week that May. Reunited at the big-league level last year, Chicago native Mallee has been a constant in Crow-Armstrong’s quest to be his best.
“That’s my baseball dad in a sense, somebody knowing you when it comes to this kind of thing, I mean, you really need it,” Crow-Armstrong told the Tribune. “I think we speak the same language. I’m lucky that I don’t have to get to know him again or anything. He knows what he’s getting into when it’s a game like that, and he knows that I always feel like there’s something we’ve got to f−−−−−− figure out. We’ve got to do it now, and he’s always down for the challenge.
“There really is no ego with him, and he’s got a lot to give, and he loves this s−−− so much. And I think, yeah, we both kind of share the same craziness sometimes when it comes to learning the game and continuously just trying to figure this s−−− out.”
Mallee knows what makes Crow-Armstrong tick, the moments to lend an ear to his frustrations and the times to get a little stern with him.
Their post-plate-appearance conversations at the dugout railing have become a staple of how Crow-Armstrong reflects and breaks down what went right or wrong. Mallee always stands in the same spot for any player who wants to get an opinion or discuss their approach ahead of their next at-bat. With Crow-Armstrong, he wants to help accelerate the development of his at-bats. Rather than focusing on whether he got a hit or not, it centers on: What was the process? Was it the right one? Do we need to change it for the next at-bat? What was the approach? Do we need to adjust?
“It allows him to process it back, go through it, and pay attention to it because the game will teach you how to play if you pay attention to it,” Mallee said to the Tribune. “Most guys will make an out and go, ‘I struck out’ or ‘I swung at a bad pitch.’ But what led into that? It’s a deeper thing for him to get a good approach and a plan, whether good or bad, rehearsing what just happened.
“The more we can put pitchers in buckets, like certain left-handed pitchers with sinkers and sweepers, then we have a general plan of how we want to approach this type of guy with this type of stuff.”
Mallee has had a front-row seat to Crow-Armstrong’s evolution over the last four years — and has helped lay the foundation for his superstardom.
“It is a special relationship,” president of baseball operations Jed Hoyer said to the Tribune. “He has a way of getting through to Pete from a hitting standpoint. He also has a way of getting through to Pete from an emotional standpoint, and I think that both of those help him immensely. You have to learn to deal with the failure of the game, and the hitting coach, a lot of their job is knowing the player and knowing what they respond to emotionally.”
When he thinks back to their time in Triple A together, the moment that stands out the most to Crow-Armstrong has nothing to do with hitting.
The day Crow-Armstrong got the call for his first big-league promotion on Sept. 11, 2023, Mallee came to Principal Park in Des Moines to say goodbye and wish him well. Pete’s mom, Ashley Crow, happened to be there too. As Crow-Armstrong headed to the airport to join the Cubs in Denver, where he debuted later that night as a pinch runner, Mallee drove his mother back to the hotel. They sat getting to know each other for an hour before Ashley Crow went to Denver.
Mallee had already left a strong impression on Crow-Armstrong during their five-plus months grinding together in Iowa, but “that kind of sold me on who I was working with.”
The coach remembers that day clearly. He went to the ballpark knowing Crow-Armstrong was getting called up and wanted to give him advice on what to expect in the majors: how to act when he arrives in the clubhouse, what his role would be, making sure he knew to go talk to then-manager David Ross right away, to listen and ask questions.
“To be honest with you, I don’t think he was ready — he was needed, but he wasn’t ready,” Mallee told the Tribune. “Talent-wise, of course, but performance-wise, there were so many different things he still needed to work on.”
But that time chatting with Ashley Crow proved pivotal in helping Mallee understand her son outside of baseball and who he is away from the field. He learned a lot about Crow-Armstrong through his mother’s eyes. He loves to win. He cares. He is genuine. He doesn’t play for the money. The team’s performance matters more than his own numbers. Mallee’s experience coaching in the minors taught him that knowing the person can be as important as helping refine a hitter’s approach or swing at that level.
“We’re all in this together, like, the mom and dad, we’ve all got to be pulling from the same side of the rope,” Mallee explained. “So if there’s things that I think at home they should talk with him about, or things to leave him alone about that really bother him and try to get the whole group because it takes a lot of people, man. It takes a lot of love and people around you that care about you and knowing they’re going to tell you the truth.
“He likes to be coached, he likes to be disciplined, he wants to be held accountable. And accepting failure is not an option. We have to somehow accept it somewhat, but never be content.”
Mallee, 57, is in his 31st season as a professional baseball coach and in his second stint with the Cubs. A graduate of Mount Carmel, Mallee was drafted out of UIC in 1991 by the Philadelphia Phillies in the 12th round and played two seasons of minor-league ball. He started his coaching career in 1996 as the Low-A Beloit hitting coach in the Milwaukee Brewers organization, a journey that took him to the Marlins, Blue Jays, Astros, Cubs, Phillies, Angels and back to Chicago.
Mallee has worked most notably with Miguel Cabrera, Jose Altuve, Kyle Schwarber, Kris Bryant, Bryce Harper, Mike Trout and Shohei Ohtani. How he describes his years working with multiple future Hall of Famers isn’t lost on Crow-Armstrong and other Cubs hitters. It’s always framed as what he took away from working with them and not “here’s what I taught them.”
“He’s just got a tremendous library of working with some of the best to ever do it,” manager Craig Counsell told the Tribune. “You’re talking about Ohtani and Trout and Harper, right? And I think John’s at a place in his career where he’s the best coach he’s ever been. I really believe that, and I think Pete benefits from that. Their personalities match each other. They’re both kind of fiery individuals, and that means the conversations are interesting and not without emotion, and I think it works for both of them.”
Coaching staff turnover is part of sports, and hitting coaches tend to get a lot of blame when things aren’t going well — and not much credit when they play an important role behind the scenes. Trust is imperative.
“Pete is going to be a good major leaguer no matter what, but I think his time with (Mallee) has really pushed him not only to be good but to be great,” second baseman Nico Hoerner told the Tribune. “(Mallee) has held him to a really high standard, and not just to be a center fielder that is going to play great defense and then maybe he’s OK with the bat or something. It’s amazing the different directions Pete’s career could have gone, and I think he’d have been great no matter what. But (Mallee) has really held him to the highest standard to be great, and I think that matches up with Pete’s mindset too.
“You need that ability to both lift people up and then also be honest and accountable,” Hoerner continued. “I think for all of us, hitting is definitely an emotional thing from the highest of highs and lowest lows, and just getting to the best version of yourself every day for 162. So to have someone in your corner like that, who knows both where you want to go, but also where you’re coming from and the background that you have, and off-the-field things that you can be open with, all of that plays into being the best version of yourself for four or five at-bats a day.”
From their first interaction in spring training 2023, Mallee saw something special in Crow-Armstrong.
He also recognized the anger and frustration whenever the budding star experienced failure; he was the same way as a player. Making an out or falling short at something was not an option for Mallee and when he did, he didn’t know how to handle it, “so I would explode with anger.”
“He is more intense and fiery than any player I have coached,” Mallee said of Crow-Armstrong. “He had what I call the ‘It’ factor like some of the great players I was fortunate enough to coach. His instincts on the field and in the box are exceptional. He has grown so much over the years and I have been blessed to be part of this journey with him.”
That understanding and relatability have been invaluable.
“I don’t think that there’s anything he’s afraid to say to me, or he’s not afraid of how to say anything to me, and there’s no tiptoeing around, nothing like that,” Crow-Armstrong said. “If anything, sometimes I feel like we cancel each other out, like, in a good way. I mean, he’s also a f−−−−−− pro and an adult, like, he’s not gonna match my energy level. He’s just gonna hopefully try and cut the fuse.”
The connection between Mallee and Crow-Armstrong speaks to the dynamic the Cubs have cultivated at the big-league level. Hitting coach Dustin Kelly has emphasized since he was hired before the 2023 season that the focus is always on the players.
“The players have egos, you have an ego, but you can’t let it come through, you have to always be there for the player, and the player is the most important. We have to be egoless,” Kelly said. “Everybody’s going to have players that they mesh with better and that they work with better. You have to delegate in this position, and if you can’t delegate, one, you’re not going to sleep, and, two, you’re just not going to give the players what they really need and deserve.”
The first six weeks of this season didn’t exactly quell concerns about Crow-Armstrong’s struggles to end last year.
Through the first 54 games, Crow-Armstrong owned a .223/.311/.363 slash line with six home runs. The 24-year-old was getting caught in between with his timing on fastballs and offspeed pitches. His plate discipline again featured too much chase. In the spring, Mallee had told Crow-Armstrong that after cutting out his leg kick in favor of a toe tap during 2025, he might end up reincorporating it this year because he developed a cleaner, more adjustable swing. Eventually the leg kick was added back, but smaller and more controlled. Crow-Armstrong’s stride timing remained inconsistent but adjustable.
“What he lacks in timing he can make up in bat speed,” Mallee said. “What the leg kick did was allow him to start very early and move towards the pitcher in a slow and controlled linear move. … It is no longer a violent crash forward but a smooth flow. Then when his eyes tell him it’s time to swing, his foot goes into the ground. His adjustability is incredible and now he can be on a 100 mph fastball and downshift to offspeed. This is when he took off.”
Those tweaks, combined with a move to the leadoff spot, put Crow-Armstrong on a tear and led to his second All-Star selection. In his last 102 games, dating to May 26, he’s posted a .307/.398/.679 line with 25 doubles, 39 home runs, 84 RBIs and a 1.077 OPS.
“I think this year showed me how long the season really is,” Crow-Armstrong said. “Last year, the struggle was a couple weeks at the beginning of the year. This was over a month. And now it feels we’ve been on this good run for a long, long time. So I think I’ve just understood how long the season actually is.”
His 2025 second-half decline highlighted what he needed to do to become more consistent in his mechanical work and game planning. Mallee recalls when first working with Crow-Armstrong at Triple A he had a “see-ball, hit-ball” approach and didn’t really use the scouting reports. Now Crow-Armstrong studiously looks at how lefties pitch to left-handed hitters and the way he’s been attacked in the past. He regularly talks about approaches with his teammates and goes up to the plate with a plan. Experience matters, too. Getting to see pitchers more frequently over the course of his career gives Crow-Armstrong a better understanding of what to look for.
“When we first started, he couldn’t even evaluate his misses,” Mallee said. “Now he’s got the pitchers in the buckets. He knows how to read the scouting reports. He knows how to anticipate, and he’s very good instinctively. Sometimes he can feel and sense. And I said, honor your gut, man. You have these instincts, buddy. They’re given to you. If you feel like something’s going to happen, then honor it and stay with it and then trust it. And if it doesn’t come out that way, it’s OK because you had a plan.”
Although he will likely always be on the higher side of swing rates, Crow-Armstrong made a change in May to not go out of the zone just because he’s capable of getting to those pitches. By July 27, he had tallied more walks this season than the previous three big-league years combined.
“I am a lot more repeatable this year, I can go into the cage and I can know that I’m going to do the same three things before I swing,” Crow-Armstrong said. “Whereas last year, there was something new every day. Other than that, though, yeah, it’s all mental.”
The power production started to emerge in abundance last year, surprising some around the league that the speedy, elite defender put up 31 home runs. That didn’t surprise Cubs assistant general manager Jared Banner. He got his first in-person look at Crow-Armstrong shortly after the New York Mets drafted him at No. 19 in 2020. Banner, the Mets’ executive director of player development at that time, had only seen some video of Crow-Armstrong play because the COVID-19 pandemic cut short his high school senior season. During a camp scrimmage at the Mets’ complex in Port St. Lucie, Fla., Crow-Armstrong slugged a home run with a 107 mph exit velocity.
It immediately grabbed Banner’s attention.
“That’s just not something you see very often from a high school kid who’s not a huge monster, just freakish power for someone of that size,” Banner said to the Tribune. “It gave me a sense that he had a ton of capacity to impact the baseball. He was already strong and had bat speed, but as he continues to grow up and mature then he’s going to hit the ball even harder. And once you’re up in that territory, it’s a leap.”
A torn labrum in his right shoulder six games into his pro career ended his 2021 season with surgery and, by keeping him under the radar with the lack of game action, helped the Cubs acquire Crow-Armstrong at the trade deadline that year.
“I think Pete always knew he was a superstar, it was the rest of us that had to catch up,” Banner said. “Superstars know how to handle the attention. They know how to handle the pressure. Heavy is the head that wears a crown, and he wears it really well.”
Crow-Armstrong has already broken multiple franchise records. One more remains in play for the final six games of the regular season. With two more stolen bases, he will become just the seventh player in MLB history to record a 40-home-run, 40-steal season.
“Stats-wise, where I’m at now, I frame it as if I keep playing well, then we’re probably gonna be in pretty good shape. But I can appreciate the persistence I’ve had and kind of the calm that I found. I guess I always know that I’m going to turn it on at some point, but I’m proud of how I did this year. I think it was a very honest showing all year of everything.”
Crow-Armstrong’s frustrations from that late August series in Arizona didn’t last long.
Back at Wrigley Field after an off day, he collected two singles against the Cincinnati Reds and then went off: a three-home-run game Aug. 29 and two more home runs the following game. Crow-Armstrong experienced a newfound satisfaction that even though he endured a tough West Coast trip not long after a 3-for-28 stretch earlier in August, he kept things in perspective.
Two tough weeks don’t have to define a season.
“One thing that I’ve talked about with people is the best players really minimize how long their poor periods are,” Crow-Armstrong said. “And I’ve started to kind of notice that where if I’m feeling really s−−−−− for a couple days, I’m making sure, and I don’t know how I do it, but I’m making sure that it’s only a couple days, and I salvaged that third day, or that fourth day, or that fifth day. I let s−−− snowball last year, and that’s not going to happen to me. I’m not willing to do that.”
His incredible performance this year has reached the point of shifting the question from whether Crow-Armstrong is the NL MVP to whether he will be unanimously chosen by the 30 Baseball Writers’ Association of America voters, something that has happened only 10 times in the National League since this iteration of the award started in 1931. The individual honor awaiting him in November is something he’s still grappling with and trying not to think about, let alone wanting to discuss, even with the regular season nearly complete.
“Someone’s gonna have to teach me what an individual season really means if stuff doesn’t really roll our way (in the playoffs),” Crow-Armstrong said. “I think that’s probably the hardest part about a win or a loss is, regardless, I’m going to focus on one of the two and probably take away from the individual stuff. But as long as I gave people something to look forward to going to the park, then that’s a big enough win for me, I think, with all the individual season stuff.”
Nearly four years before Crow-Armstrong was born, Sammy Sosa played a big role in creating the next generation of Cubs fans during his electric 66-home-run 1998 season that culminated in the NL MVP award. For him to do something at that level this year, for such a historic franchise, must feel surreal, right?
“I don’t want to believe it just yet,” Crow-Armstrong said. “So when we get there, you can ask me.”

item.content:encoded:
It might seem like I am an eternal pessimist, but I do believe there are silver linings in every cloud. The Houston Astros got swept by the Atlanta Braves and now trail the Texas Rangers by a game for the AL West crown, and the Chicago White Sox by two games for the last wild card spot. They are going to two cities they do not play well in. In terms of the playoff chase, it does not look good for the hometown nine.
However, behind every challenge is an opportunity. Make no mistake, I am not predicting victory at all. I don't see this road trip going well for a number of reasons. I think a 2-4 finish is likely in the offing and that should not be enough to win the AL West or advance to the wild card. I would be personally ashamed to finish 79-83 and advance to the postseason. However, failing to make the postseason two years in a row and dropping below .500 opens up an opportunity for Jim Crane and company.
They have already jettisoned Dana Brown. They will also jettison Joe Espada if all reporting is true. It is fundamentally impossible to justify keeping him after fading horribly down the stretch. So, how is this an opportunity? Simply put, this team has been hanging on for years. Dusty Baker was a caretaker that just happened to last four seasons. Dana Brown wasn't a serious hire meant to change the direction of the franchise. They just hoped to limp along and see the good times roll.
Espada himself was essentially seen as an extension of Baker. He was a guy that the players seemed to like and they thought that hanging out with Baker since 2020 would rub off on him and keep the magic going. It worked through 2024. Failing this season and failing in the way that they have forces change. Real change. You have a new guy coming in on top and he will hire people under him to usher him.
Change is never easy and often scary, but it brings with it opportunity for the Astros to get things right in the front office and the dugout to stop the downward slide.
It won't be easy. Jose Altuve, Carlos Correa, and Christian Walker are all in their mid thirties and highly paid. They aren't likely to get better and more than likely will be a year worse and not a year better. They are roughly making a combined 70 million dollars as well. That is nearly a third of your payroll. A new GM will have to make some dramatic moves because this team is beyond minor tweaks. A new regime gives new opportunities to do that.
It also presents an opportunity to really beat the bushes to hire a new manager. The inside track shouldn't be a part of this equation. They can interview experienced former managers and the younger former players that seem to be the new wave of managers. Again, this is an opportunity for some creativity and a thoughtful process that can produce the best guy for this roster and the roster we will likely have in the next few seasons.
I want my team to win and will always root for them to win, but a part of me is frightened by that outcome. I am frightened by the prospect of winning a horrible division and having that convince Crane and company that they are on the right track. This team has been getting steadily worse since they won the World Series in 2022. Some of that is the natural aging process. Some of that are key players from that team that have moved on. However, most of it is a regime that has kicked the can down the road and spun its wheels because of a lack of vision and a lack of autonomy.
New voices in the front office can solve both of those issues if they are allowed to. Jim Crane has long talked about the importance of winning. He consistently has spent more money than any other owner in Astros history since they have been on the run. He commits plenty of financial resources. It is time to stop the brain drain and bring back smart baseball. The opportunity is there for the taking and now there is no excuse not to get it done.

item.content:encoded:
Bobby Witt Jr. is having a down year. He’s running his worst batting line in three seasons. He’s in danger of missing the 20-homer threshold for the first time in his career. A lower back injury in July will also limit him to a career low in games played. Put it together, and Witt is on pace to put up his the lowest WAR total since his 5.9-win 2023 campaign. Oh, and he also grabbed hold of the American League lead in WAR back in July and still hasn’t relinquished it. A down year by Bobby Witt Jr.’s standards is still good enough to make him a deserving MVP.
I don’t know if Witt is going to win his first MVP this year. Ours is the only flavor of WAR in which he leads the AL, and he leads by just a quarter of a win. He ranks third by Baseball Reference’s rWAR and is eighth by Baseball Prospectus’ WARP. Yordan Alvarez leads all of baseball in WARP because he’s hitting like, well, Yordan Alvarez and staying healthy like, well, someone other than Yordan Alvarez. Cam Schlittler leads the AL in Baseball Reference WAR, and he’s been so dominant that he deserves consideration for the Cy Young-MVP combo — if only he’d pitched just 23 fewer innings last year, he could’ve gone for the trifecta with Rookie of the Year. Kevin McGonigle has played like an MVP from the moment he arrived in Detroit, and Junior Caminero has surpassed 40 home runs for the second season in a row as a 23-year-old. All of these guys have a case, and they aren’t the only ones who merit inclusion in the discussion:

Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, Schlittler, McGonigle and JJ Wetherholt have made the AL MVP the only major award that’s really in question). If you want to read a particularly good example, you should check out the one Mario Delgado Genzor wrote for Baseball Prospectus on Friday. I want to focus on something slightly different — namely, how good Witt has already been in years when he missed out on an MVP and how unusual it would be for him to win it this year.
(A quick note before we get into it: We’re about to spend a lot of time talking about WAR. I know I mentioned rWAR and WARP earlier. They’re an important piece of the puzzle, especially due to the outsized effect rWAR in particular has on the MVP conversation, but from here on out, we’re sticking with good old FanGraphs WAR.)
This is Witt’s fifth major league season, and you could argue that it’s his fourth consecutive MVP-caliber campaign. Mind you, that argument would focus only on 2022, in which he put up 5.9 WAR, good for 10th in the majors. There’s no argument to be had about the 2024 and 2025 seasons. That said, along with Shohei Ohtani’s combined 9.2-WAR 2022 sesaon, they are the two most valuable seasons this decade for which a position player did not win an MVP. In 2024, Witt ran a 169 wRC+, stole 31 bases, and put up a Fielding Run Value of 11, fourth among all shortstops. That was good for 10.5 WAR, and it took the best season of Aaron Judge’s career – 58 home runs, a 19% walk rate, and a .322 batting average – to beat him. In 2025, Witt put up 8.0 WAR with a 130 wRC+, 38 steals, and 20 FRV, the best mark among all shortstops. Again, he was bested by a 10-win season from Judge and Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer campaign. Witt has never received a first place MVP vote.
Crow-Armstrong, who has the National League MVP all but locked down, gives us a great example of what it normally takes to win an MVP award. He may even finish with 10.5 WAR through his excellence in all three phases of the game, just like Witt did in 2024. Players like Judge, Ohtani, and Mike Trout, whose base level of talent is so high that a healthy campaign is almost sure to keep them a step above the rest of the league, don’t come around all that often. Even when they do come around, they still need to be playing at something close to their peak, and peaks don’t last that long. Until Ohtani, the only player to win more than three MVPs was Barry Bonds, whose regimen for raising and widening his peak has been well documented. Sometimes that’s because of voter fatigue, but often it’s because somebody else popped up with an amazing, undeniable season like PCA’s. Most of the time, the MVP is an already great player for whom everything goes perfectly. They stay healthy and they play not just their best, but over their heads. Think of Ronald Acuña Jr. winning the NL MVP in 2023 with 9.1 WAR, 4.1 more than his next-best total, or Mookie Betts winning the AL MVP in 2018 with 10.2 WAR, 2.8 more than his next-best total.
Generally speaking, since the voting started getting more rigorous in the last couple decades, those are the two categories of players who win MVPs. We see all-time greats who perform like only they are capable of performing, and we see excellent players who put it all together in a blaze of glory. Witt’s 2024 season probably falls into that second category. He wasn’t quite at his defensive or baserunning peak, but he put up his best season at the plate by nearly 40 points of wRC+ and DRC+, and he ended up with an all-timer of a season. His 10.5 WAR tied for the 36th-best position player campaign of all time. His company? Willie Mays and Babe Ruth twice apiece, Barry Bonds, and Rogers Hornsby. Unfortunately, he ran into one of those special players from the first category, in the form of Judge. If Witt had put up those 2024 numbers this year, he’d be en route to a unanimous MVP just like PCA.
But I said “in theory” earlier, and I said it because Witt isn’t done yet. He’s still just 26, and if not for those weeks he missed with back tightness, or a wOBA that’s more than 30 points below his xwOBA, he’d now be wrapping up his third straight seven-plus-win season. He’s elite in every facet of the game and he doesn’t look like he’s in danger of slowing down any time soon. It wouldn’t be much of a shock to see him rediscover his nine- or 10-win form. In other words, there’s at least a chance Witt belongs to that first category of player and not the second.
Earlier I mentioned Acuña and Betts claiming MVPs by putting up the best years of their careers by a long shot. That’s pretty standard. Especially in recent years, it’s awfully rare for a player to take home an MVP award in something other than the best season of their career, unless they also won the MVP in the best year of their career. Leaving those multi-time MVPs out (and excluding 2020 for obvious reasons), here’s the whole list of players who won an MVP in a year that wasn’t their best by fWAR since 2011: Giancarlo Stanton and Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt put up 6.8 WAR in his 2022 NL MVP season and 7.2 in 2015. In that sense, Goldschmidt fit a third archetype: the established star who doesn’t put up their biggest WAR total, and instead wins MVP as something of a career achievement award. Stanton put up 6.5 WAR in 2017, not quite the 6.8-win campaign he put up in 2014, but he was facing a weaker field, he was more established as a star, and he had the cachet of a 59-homer season. We’re talking about gaps of less than half a win. We had some multi-time winners, but Acuña, Betts, Cody Bellinger, Christian Yelich, Jose Altuve, Kris Bryant, Josh Donaldson, Andrew McCutchen, and Buster Posey all won MVP in the best seasons of their career by fWAR.
Let’s say that Witt does win the MVP this year. For the sake of round numbers, let’s say he closes strong and finishes with 7.0 WAR. That would be just the third-best season of his career, and a full 3.5 WAR below his career-high. Baseball Reference lists MVP winners going back to 1911, and in that time, Witt would become just the ninth position player to win MVP in a season that trailed their best year by such a wide margin. The list of players to do it before him is full of three-time MVPs like Joe DiMaggio, Mickey Mantle, and Mike Schmidt. Not only that, but you’ll note that if Witt does make this list, the only higher number in either column will belong to Mantle:
| Player | MVP Year | MVP WAR | Best Year | Best WAR | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frankie Frisch | 1931 | 4.1 | 1927 | 9.7 | 5.6 |
| Mickey Mantle | 1962 | 6.0 | 1956 | 11.5 | 5.5 |
| Willie Stargell | 1979 | 2.7 | 1971 | 8.2 | 5.4 |
| Joe DiMaggio | 1947 | 4.8 | 1941 | 9.7 | 4.9 |

The last person to do so was Robin Yount, who won the AL MVP with 9.8 WAR in 1982, and then again with 5.3 WAR in 1989, long before anybody knew that Total Zone considered him the 11th-worst defender in the majors. This hasn’t happened in nearly 30 years, and Witt is in a very different boat here. He’s not one of the two MVP favorites because his season looks great to the eye but doesn’t fool the advanced metrics. He’s not an aging star who can count on some lifetime-achievement votes. He’s a young gun who’s leading his league in WAR because he excels in every facet of the game.
I realize that this is far from the most meticulous analysis I’ve ever conducted, and that MVP voting is and should be about more than WAR. Still, I hope I’ve put this season in the context it deserves. By our measuring stick, Witt has been the best player in the American League this season. He’s done so despite missing time due to injury. He’s done so despite some bad batted ball luck. And he’s done so despite not even coming close to the highest gear we know he’s got available to him, because that gear is so high that it’s normally reserved for inner-circle Hall of Famers. However the voting goes, Witt’s been in MVP form for three or four years now.

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox were unable to punch their own ticket to the postseason Sunday, as they fell to the Tampa Bay Rays, 5-1, at Tropicana Field.
Fortunately, one of their former pitchers, the grandson of one of the greatest players to ever don a Red Sox uniform and Boston’s original major league team did it for them.
With a 4-2 defeat of the Houston Astros late Sunday afternoon, the Atlanta Braves propelled the Red Sox to October.
Left-hander Martin Pérez, who pitched for the 2020-21 Red Sox, started for the Braves and held the Astros to one run, a solo homer by Jose Altuve, over 4 1/3 innings.
But the biggest Boston-connected contribution came from Mike Yastrzemski, grandson of Red Sox icon Carl Yastrzemski and a former Red Sox late-round draft pick out of St. John’s Prep in Danvers, Ma. The younger Yaz’s three-run homer in the sixth gave the Braves an enduring lead, and the Red Sox an in.
His momentous home run also coincided with the 59th anniversary of his grandfather hitting his 41st home run and scoring the go-ahead run to keep the 1967 “Impossible Dream” Red Sox in a first-place tie with the Minnesota Twins in a tight American League pennant race.
The final piece of this New England-centric puzzle was a game-ending strikeout of Astros shortstop Jeremy Pena. The Braves originally drafted him in the 39th round of the 2015 MLB Draft out of Providence’s Classic High School, before the Astros took him in the third round in 2018, out of the University of Maine.
The Red Sox watched the Braves from the visitors’ clubhouse at Tropicana Field, then donned “Clinched” t-shirts and goggles, and went back out to the field to celebrate and give the attendants time to seal the clubhouse in plastic wrap and wheel in the champagne and beer.
Long before the Red Sox played their inaugural season as one of the American League’s eight charter clubs in 1901, Boston had the Braves. The Braves were originally the Red Stockings, their name from their 1871 inception until 1876, when they were renamed the Red Caps until 1882.
The 1914 Boston Braves were the first team in MLB history to reach the postseason after being 14 games under .500 at some point in the season. It was a feat only matched by the 1974 Pittsburgh Pirates and 2005 Astros.
Until Sunday, when the Braves helped the Red Sox become the fourth team to do so.

Hunter Brown hit his glove with his right hand to celebrate the excellent catch by second baseman Nick Allen, who took Matt Olson out of the play. The fifth inning had ended and, once again, Brown did his part of the plan with five scoreless innings, 10 strikeouts for the fifth time in his last 10 starts and just three hits allowed.
On the other hand, the Houston Astros could not respond. Brown left the game with a minimal 1-0 lead thanks to a solo home run by José Altuve in the bottom of the fourth inning against Atlanta Braves left-hander Martín Pérez. Once the bullpen came into action, the Braves turned the score around with a four-run rally in the top of the sixth inning.
The story was repeating itself. It is Brown’s 11th consecutive start in which he has reached at least five innings. During that stretch, he is 5-2 with an improvement to a 2.76 ERA compared to his 4.05 ERA in his first eight starts of this year. However, the Astros have wasted four of his dominant starts without being able to take advantage of the impact of their main rotation ace.
Before Sunday’s game, Houston’s last at-home game in this regular season, the team was 9-9 in Brown’s starts. In eight of those losses, they scored four or fewer runs. Brown has continued to throw between 90 and 100 pitches in each of his last seven outings, and he has made significant adjustments at this key moment when Houston is playing for the Division lead against the Texas Rangers as the priority, or, if they lose the top spot, at least a spot in the Wild Card Series.
A look at Brown’s significant adjustments
Sunday’s start was the typical outing in the style of the Hunter Brown, who finished third in the Cy Young Award voting last year: a large number of swings and misses, control of the upper part of the strike zone and that ability to attack hitters. Brown began with a strike to 15 of the 21 opponents he faced and got at least one strikeout with five of the seven types of pitches he threw. Three came with the sinker and four-seam fastball, while generating a 53.8% swing-and-miss rate (seven of 13) with his mix of knuckle curveball, cutter and changeup.
If we compare two key stretches that define Brown’s return to dominance, there are very interesting differences between his first eight starts and these last 10.
Without a doubt, Brown’s most significant change is in the sinker. In his first eight starts, it was largely a pitch to tie up the hitter. 41.6% of the swings resulted in tied up, but the problem was that it produced just 13% whiffs. As his main pitch, Brown needed to find the upper part of the zone where he has usually dominated and make hitters chase the sinker at the corners of the zone.
The adjustment got underway to the point that, in his last 10 starts, tied up swings dropped to 18.6%, flailed doubled (32.6%) and whiff has risen to 26.4%. That explains part of another result, and it has been the improvement in late swings during this recent stretch. When the sinker reaches this point and breaks hitters’ timing, Brown’s entire arsenal around it becomes more effective thanks to the great contrast of his knuckle curveball, cutter and changeup.
The curve also took an important step, further improving its swing-and-miss rate from 30.5% to 38.7%. As you can see in the table, the four-seam shows another type of evolution. It continues generating a similar whiff rate (23.4%), but Perfect Contact fell from 24.7% to 15.6%. The more Brown’s arsenal works, the smaller the opponents’ margin for error becomes as his pitches create different problems.
The bad news for Brown is that the Astros still cannot take enough advantage of his starts, and the bullpen has wasted the win probability that his dominance is generating. The Astros will face a finish that could seem easy, but in reality, their results against the Athletics and Mariners have been puzzling: against both opponents, the team is 6-14 this season, with a –16 run differential.

HOUSTON (AP) Ronald Acuña Jr. hit a go-ahead grand slam in the seventh inning, and the Atlanta Braves beat Houston 6-3 Saturday night to drop the Astros out of the AL West lead.
Houston (77-78) fell one game behind Texas (78-77) and trails the Chicago White Sox (79-76) by two games for the last AL wild card. The Astros had held at least a share of the division lead each day since Aug. 25.
Atlanta assured its eighth playoff berth in nine seasons on Friday and is in position to clinch its first NL East title since 2023 on Sunday.
Trailing 2-1, Atlanta loaded the bases against AJ Blubaugh (5-3) and Acuña homered off Bryan Abreu for his second grand slam this season and the fifth of his big league career.
Acuña singled and walked twice in his first three plate appearances. He has homered in three of his last four games.
Mike Yastrzemski added a solo homer in the eighth inning.
Grant Holmes (10-5) allowed two runs and eight hits over six innings.
Yainer Diaz hit an RBI double in the eighth off Dylan Lee, who struck out pinch-hitter Nelson Velázquez to end the inning.
Raisel Iglesias pitched a perfect ninth inning for his 34th save in 37 chances.
Jose Altuve had three hits for Houston, while Isaac Paredes was 2 for 3 with a home run, walk and two RBIs.
Christian Walker had two hits after entering the game hitless in his previous 23 at-bats.
Hayden Wesneski allowed one run on four hits over 5 1/3 innings.
Astros RHP Hunter Brown (6-3, 3.43 ERA) and Braves LHP Martín Pérez (9-9, 3.07 ERA) start Sunday.
